props.title: Night of the Creeps
props.initialSlug: Alien slugs turn college kids into zombie hosts

sections.content: Night of the Creeps brilliantly mashes up 1950s alien invasion films with 1980s slasher comedy. Director Fred Dekker crafted this cult classic as a love letter to classic horror, naming characters after famous genre directors like Romero, Raimi, and Carpenter. The film's alien brain parasites and zombie outbreak narrative draws from Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) while its college setting and sharp humor prefigures Scream (1996) and The Faculty (1998).

sections.content: Tom Atkins delivers an iconic performance as Detective Ray Cameron, whose "thrill me" catchphrase became legendary among horror fans. The film's practical effects by David B. Miller, who worked on An American Werewolf in London (1981), hold up remarkably well. The zombie cats and exploding heads showcase the height of 1980s practical effects craftsmanship, influencing later horror-comedies like Dead Alive (1992) and Bad Taste (1987).

The film's greatest strength lies in its genre-bending approach, seamlessly blending sci-fi horror with teen comedy elements years before Tremors (1990) or The Faculty (1998). Dekker's script balances genuine scares with sharp dialogue and memorable characters, creating a template for later horror-comedies like Idle Hands (1999) and Slither (2006). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: Night of the Creeps helped establish the horror-comedy hybrid that would dominate the late 1980s and early 1990s. Its influence can be seen in everything from Army of Darkness (1992) to Buffy the Vampire Slayer (1992). The film's strategic use of practical effects over CGI influenced modern filmmakers like James Wan and Ti West, who continue to emphasize practical effects in films like Malignant (2021) and X (2022).
